sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Welcome. Today's story is about a man who received a clear message from God — and immediately ran the other way. It's the story of Jonah, and it's told in a short book of just four chapters. Most people remember the great fish. But the fish is not really the main point. This is a story about God's mercy: mercy for a runaway prophet, and mercy for a city full of people Jonah didn't think deserved it.

As you listen, ask yourself: are there people I secretly hope God won't be merciful to?

sections.title: The Story, Part 1
sections.text:
The book begins: the word of the Lord came to Jonah, saying, “Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.” Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, a powerful and violent empire, and one of Israel's worst enemies.

But Jonah didn't want to go. Jonah chapter one, verse three tells us: “But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it.” Tarshish was in the opposite direction from Nineveh, about as far west as a person could sail. Notice how many times the word down appears. Jonah went down to Joppa, down into the ship, and soon he would go down even further.

Then the Lord sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty storm, so that the ship was about to break apart. The sailors were terrified. Each one cried out to his own god, and they threw cargo overboard to lighten the ship. And where was Jonah? Fast asleep in the bottom of the ship. The captain woke him and said, get up and call on your God!

The sailors cast lots to find out who was to blame, and the lot fell on Jonah. He confessed, “I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land.” He told them he was running from the Lord. Then he said, take me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will be calm. The sailors tried hard to row back to land, but the storm only grew worse. Finally, they prayed to the Lord and threw Jonah overboard, and the sea stopped raging. The sailors feared the Lord greatly and offered sacrifices to Him.

sections.title: The Story, Part 2
sections.text:
Jonah chapter one, verse seventeen: “Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.”

From inside the fish, Jonah prayed. He remembered sinking into the deep, with the weeds wrapped about his head. And he ended his prayer with these words: “But I will sacrifice unto thee with the voice of thanksgiving; I will pay that that I have vowed. Salvation is of the LORD.” Then the Lord spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land.

Then comes one of the most hopeful verses in the book: “And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time.” God gave him a second chance. This time, Jonah went to Nineveh. He walked through the city crying out, “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”

And something amazing happened. The people of Nineveh believed God. They proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. Even the king rose from his throne, took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. He commanded everyone to cry mightily to God and to turn from their evil ways and their violence. He said, who can tell if God will turn and relent? Jonah chapter three, verse ten: “And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.”

You might expect Jonah to be thrilled. Instead, he was very angry. He prayed, “I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness.” In other words, this is exactly why I ran! I knew You would forgive them.

Jonah went outside the city and sat down to see what would happen. God prepared a plant — the Bible calls it a gourd — to grow up and shade Jonah's head, and Jonah was very glad. But the next morning God prepared a worm that attacked the plant, and it withered. Then came a hot east wind and a blazing sun, and Jonah was so miserable he wished to die. God asked him, you had pity on a plant you didn't plant or grow. Should I not spare Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and also much cattle? And the book ends with that question hanging in the air.

sections.title: The Lesson
sections.text:
What does Jonah teach us?

First, you can't outrun God. Jonah tried to flee from the presence of the Lord, but God followed him onto the ship, into the sea, and into the belly of the fish. That's not a threat — it's good news. Wherever you go, God's love can reach you.

Second, God gives second chances. The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time. If you have run from God, it is not too late to turn around.

Third, God's mercy is bigger than our prejudices. Jonah wanted mercy for himself but judgment for his enemies. God loved the people of Nineveh. And He loves the people we find hardest to love.

And finally, Jesus Himself pointed to this story. He said that as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so He would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth — a picture of His death and resurrection. Salvation truly is of the Lord.

sections.title: Prayer and Reflection
sections.text:
Is there someone you struggle to want God to bless? Is there something God has asked of you that you've been running from? Take a quiet moment to be honest with God about it.

Let's pray. Gracious God, thank You that You are merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness. Thank You for second chances. Forgive me for the times I have run from You, and give me a heart that wants Your mercy for others as much as for myself. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Thank you for listening. Next time, we'll hear about Daniel, a young man who stayed faithful far from home.
